messages.subject: Conversion of classes "difftime", "Date" and "POSIXct" in factor by unmarkedFrameOccu()
messages.subject_clean: Conversion of classes "difftime", "Date" and "POSIXct" in factor by unmarkedFrameOccu()
messages.body_plain:
Hello everybody,

I was formatting data for an occupancy model and stumbled upon something that could potentially cause issues for some analyses.

Some of the covariates I'm using for the observation process include objects of class "difftime", "POSIXct" and "Date" (for sampling duration, start and end times, and days, respectively). When using "unmarkedFrameOccu()" to format the data for "occu()", it automatically converts those classes as factors (without any warning). This should be ok for an analysis where the date is considered as a factor, but could cause problems in other situations, such as the case where survey durations are converted to factors.

As a temporary fix, you can manually convert those parameters as numerics prior inputting them in "unmarkedFrameOccu()". From what I gathered, Richard is already working on a fix for this problem. In the mean time, it can be useful to check that the classes of your covariates correspond to what you wish. A simple analysis of the structure of your unmarkedFrameOccu object (with "str()") should do the trick.

Regards,

Florent

Hi,

After fitting the model, I would like to estimate the abundance for a certain area whose point transects are a subset of the entire sample.  So far I have the following:

m1<-gdistsamp(lambdaformula = ~1, phiformula = ~1, pformula = ~time +  julian+sky+wind, data = umf, keyfun = "hazard")
re<-ranef(m1)
cis<-confint(re)

I believe this produces 95% confidence intervals for each individual point transect.  How would I construct a 95% confidence interval for the sum of the abundances for the first 10 sites?  Would we need an estimate of the posterior distribution of the sum and then use the quantiles to get the correct interval?  Should these be called confidence or credible intervals?

Thanks,

Russ

Dear Russ,

I think you should bootstrap to get that uncertainty interval.
(1) select a sample of size n from your data set of size (i.e., number of sites) n, WITH REPLACEMENT, fit the model, do any model selection you deem necessary, come up with the estimate of the total N for the first 10 sites and save it
(2) repeat this a large number of times, e.g., 1000
(3) The desired 95% interval is given by the appropriate percentiles

I think this would be called a frequentist interval, i.e., CI.

Kind regards  ---  Marc

Dear Nicole,

if the single-visit sites are a random subset from all sites, then no problem with them.

The only problem is when they are "different", for instance, less "good" sites, where population density of the critters is lower, and so people didn't want to pay a large effort at such sites where they are less likely to see things.

If this latter was true, then p would be greater in the sites with replication, which provide (almost) all info about p, and the estimate of p would be biased high and that for psi biased low.

Evan, the yearlySiteCovs and obsCovs need to be specified as lists, with each item in the list representing a single covariate that was measured at the correct temporal scale (i.e., every primary or secondary occasion).  That is how the model can use multiple covariates at each level:

yearlySiteCovs=list(year=year, climate=climate)
obsCovs=list(date=date, temp=temp)

Each item in those lists is a matrix with dimensions that match either n_sites*n_years or n_sites*n_surveys.  In my example above, year and climate are specific to the primary occasions, while date and temp are specific to the secondary occasions.  And these covariates may or may not vary across sites within the time period.

Hello,

I want to thank everyone for their helpful responses.  After talking to my collaborator about the analysis results, I had a couple of more questions regarding the models.   As a reminder, the data was collected using a distance sampling design where each point transect was visited twice a year and there was a total of two years.

Questions:

1) The model being fit using the gdistsamp function is for multiple year data where each point transect is visited once per year.  What is it about the model that makes it inappropriate to use multiple year data where each point transect is visited multiple times within a year, but it is appropriate to use for multiple year data where each point transect is visited only once per year?  What assumptions are being violated?  It seems that there is temporal correlation in each situation.

2) If we where to use the pcountOpen function for the entire data set and ignore the distance information then would the model associated with pcountOpen be valid or is there something inherit in the distance sampling design that when the distance information is ignored leads to the assumptions for the model used in the pcountOpen function being violated?

3) Would it be more appropriate it for us to use the model proposed in the paper entitled "An open population hierarchical distance sampling model" by Sollmann et al. (2015) that is to appear in Ecology.  Andy Royle and Richard Chandler are co-authors and this paper seems to have a similar feel to that of Dail and Madsen (2011).

Thanks again for everyone's help,

Russ

Dear Hill,

the way the standard dynamic occupancy model is parameterised, you cannot put something that varies as a covariate on psi.

psi is the occupancy in the first year. All the other psi's in the following years are functions of the first-year psi and the parameters for the dynamics. Only on these latter can you put yearly varying site covariates. If you want to model annually varying occupancy, then you have to do this in a different parameterisation of the model, one which is not available in unmarked. May be in PRESENCE or MARK. Or code that simpler model without explicit dynamics in BUGS.

Regards  --  Marc

         sr <- fm@sitesRemoved

HI Nicole,

The detection parameters in these two different types of model have different interpretations.

So, you would expect these values to be different, although they can be somewhat related.

Its appropriate to use both, but in context of course.

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nicole,

and the two detection probs are related like the following:

P* = 1 - (1-p)^N,

where P* is the occupancy detection probability: the prob to detect at least one of the N individuals present. That is equal to 1 minus the prob to detect none of the N of them.

Hence, whenever there are more than 1 ind. per site, the Nmix detection prob will be less than the occu detection prob.

Regards  -- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear Hemanta et al.,

I have a comment on the GOF testing using the parboot in unmarked.

In parts of the capture-recapture world, e.g., when people fit Cormack-Jolly-Seber models for survival estimation and also in some parts of the occupancy universe (I think in that part where MARK and PRESENCE lives in), it is standard practice to do some GOF test and from that compute a c.hat index, which should be 1 for a fitting model. Values greater than 1 indicate EITHER the breakdown of the model OR simply some additional noise (or both). Extra noise is called "overdispersion" and is very common with all kinds of count data. Unless c.hat is greater than about 3 or so, people then always assume that c.hat>1 indicates simply extra noise, rather than a systematic breakdown of the model, and they adjust uncertainty measures (e.g., inflate SE's by sqrt(c.hat)) and AIC model selection indices (to become QAIC). For values of c.hat in the range of 1-2, this is done almost as a rule. In MARK, c.hat is computed from a parametric bootstrap of a fit statistic as the ratio of the observed value for the actual data set and the mean of the bootstrap distribution of the fit statistic under H0 of a fitting model.

Almost every time when I have done a parboot GOF for some model in unmarked and the model did not fit (p<0.05 or even p << 0.01), the value of c.hat was less than 2 and often far less so (e.g., 1.15). So I have started to think that we should probably often do what the CJS people do and simply inflate our SEs and AIC scores accordingly. The former can easily be done using functions in the "sister package" AICcmodavg. When this is done, we also see that the inflation of the SEs with c.hat values of 1.5 or something are often pretty minimal.

Note: I am not saying that this is necessarily *always* a good thing to do, only that I don't see why this approach should be adequate for a CJS model or an occupancy model fit in PRESENCE, but not for the hierarchical models fit in unmarked.

Note 2: I think that we should do more to assess the fit of our models. Particularly important and really more important than a simple black and white answer appear model diagnostics such as residuals, which show you *where* a model fits particularly badly. Residuals can easily be computed for all models in unmarked.

I think that there remains a lot to be done to develop methods and accumulate experience about GOF in HMs such as the ones fit using unmarked.

Comments welcome !

Kind regards  --  Marc

                                                                   obsCovs = mallard.obs)
(ufm.mallard.global <- occu(~ date + I(date^2) ~ forest + elev,mallardUMF))
# examine all combinations
(d1 <- dredge(ufm.mallard.global, rank = AIC))

# Fit model with psi held constant
(ufm.mallard <- occu(~ date + I(date^2) ~ 1,mallardUMF))
# Find the best detection model
(d2 <- dredge(ufm.mallard, rank = AIC))
# keep date and date^2 in comparisons (#2 model from above)
(d2 <- dredge(ufm.mallard.global, rank = AIC,subset=`p(date)`&`p(I(date^2))`))

This just takes the mallard dataset and illustrates some model selection options.  Note the subsetting specification is a bit complex (here I used the backtick or grave accent symbol).  The dredge help file has a pretty thorough explanation of it.

Dear Hemanta et al.,

I have a comment on the GOF testing using the parboot in unmarked.

In parts of the capture-recapture world, e.g., when people fit Cormack-Jolly-Seber models for survival estimation and also in some parts of the occupancy universe (I think in that part where MARK and PRESENCE lives in), it is standard practice to do some GOF test and from that compute a c.hat index, which should be 1 for a fitting model. Values greater than 1 indicate EITHER the breakdown of the model OR simply some additional noise (or both). Extra noise is called "overdispersion" and is very common with all kinds of count data. Unless c.hat is greater than about 3 or so, people then always assume that c.hat>1 indicates simply extra noise, rather than a systematic breakdown of the model, and they adjust uncertainty measures (e.g., inflate SE's by sqrt(c.hat)) and AIC model selection indices (to become QAIC). For values of c.hat in the range of 1-2, this is done almost as a rule. In MARK, c.hat is computed from a parametric bootstrap of a fit statistic as the ratio of the observed value for the actual data set and the mean of the bootstrap distribution of the fit statistic under H0 of a fitting model.

Almost every time when I have done a parboot GOF for some model in unmarked and the model did not fit (p<0.05 or even p << 0.01), the value of c.hat was less than 2 and often far less so (e.g., 1.15). So I have started to think that we should probably often do what the CJS people do and simply inflate our SEs and AIC scores accordingly. The former can easily be done using functions in the "sister package" AICcmodavg. When this is done, we also see that the inflation of the SEs with c.hat values of 1.5 or something are often pretty minimal.

Note: I am not saying that this is necessarily *always* a good thing to do, only that I don't see why this approach should be adequate for a CJS model or an occupancy model fit in PRESENCE, but not for the hierarchical models fit in unmarked.

Note 2: I think that we should do more to assess the fit of our models. Particularly important and really more important than a simple black and white answer appear model diagnostics such as residuals, which show you *where* a model fits particularly badly. Residuals can easily be computed for all models in unmarked.

I think that there remains a lot to be done to develop methods and accumulate experience about GOF in HMs such as the ones fit using unmarked.

Comments welcome !

Kind regards  --  Marc

If you want my gut reaction, you might not like it!  But I am definitely open to being schooled by someone more knowledgeable.

The c.hat adjustments are all so ad-hoc and minimal that I don't see the point.  If c.hat suggests something is off with your model, an adjustment will not fix that.  And that is just fine, given the model is always an approximation to begin with.  If you are worried about the SEs being underestimated, that is reasonable, but the SEs are probably always underestimated for all kinds of reasons.  Some may find such adjustments critical because of implications regarding p-values and AIC, but the inferences from those statistics will always be open to interpretation.  I feel like the reporting of c.hat is most useful for recognizing that parts of the model do not fit well, which may lead to more critical thinking about the problem.  If the c.hat adjustment really changes your interpretation, you were already dealing with a lot of model uncertainty in the first place.

I am in the camp of seeing out-of-sample prediction as what really matters, even though like most ecologists, I am rarely able to do it myself.  So while I respect the decision to use c.hat adjustments however you choose and would not criticize it, I also would not criticize the choice to completely ignore such adjustments.  For me, reporting the c.hat is potentially important but using it is less so.

> Dear Hemanta et al.,
>
> I have a comment on the GOF testing using the parboot in unmarked.
>
> In parts of the capture-recapture world, e.g., when people fit Cormack-Jolly-Seber models for survival estimation and also in some parts of the occupancy universe (I think in that part where MARK and PRESENCE lives in), it is standard practice to do some GOF test and from that compute a c.hat index, which should be 1 for a fitting model. Values greater than 1 indicate EITHER the breakdown of the model OR simply some additional noise (or both). Extra noise is called "overdispersion" and is very common with all kinds of count data. Unless c.hat is greater than about 3 or so, people then always assume that c.hat>1 indicates simply extra noise, rather than a systematic breakdown of the model, and they adjust uncertainty measures (e.g., inflate SE's by sqrt(c.hat)) and AIC model selection indices (to become QAIC). For values of c.hat in the range of 1-2, this is done almost as a rule. In MARK, c.hat is computed from a parametric bootstrap of a fit statistic as the ratio of the observed value for the actual data set and the mean of the bootstrap distribution of the fit statistic under H0 of a fitting model.
>
> Almost every time when I have done a parboot GOF for some model in unmarked and the model did not fit (p<0.05 or even p << 0.01), the value of c.hat was less than 2 and often far less so (e.g., 1.15). So I have started to think that we should probably often do what the CJS people do and simply inflate our SEs and AIC scores accordingly. The former can easily be done using functions in the "sister package" AICcmodavg. When this is done, we also see that the inflation of the SEs with c.hat values of 1.5 or something are often pretty minimal.
>
> Note: I am not saying that this is necessarily *always* a good thing to do, only that I don't see why this approach should be adequate for a CJS model or an occupancy model fit in PRESENCE, but not for the hierarchical models fit in unmarked.
>
> Note 2: I think that we should do more to assess the fit of our models. Particularly important and really more important than a simple black and white answer appear model diagnostics such as residuals, which show you *where* a model fits particularly badly. Residuals can easily be computed for all models in unmarked.
>
> I think that there remains a lot to be done to develop methods and accumulate experience about GOF in HMs such as the ones fit using unmarked.
